$about: WHAT MUST BE IN THE SCENE TREE AFTER BOOT, AND WHAT MAY NOT CLAIM TO BE.
The build menu was never in the scene tree. The palette, the tech tree, the
Book of Laws, the recipe browser and the blueprint library therefore did not
exist in the running game, the society system issued ultimatums demanding a
law the player had no UI to sign, and 768 tests, a determinism replay and a
perf gate all reported green — because every one of them tests the
simulation, and none of them ever asked whether a human can reach it.
tools/reachability_probe.gd boots the real game and writes down what is
actually there. tools/check_reachability.py grades that dump against this
file. Three independent teeth, so missing one seam does not hide the others:
required[]      a subsystem that must be found, by script path or group.
claim_keywords  ANY log line that says something installed must be able to
point at the node. This is the general form of the bug:
the log said 'view installed: ... build menu ...' while the
menu sat on an orphan CanvasLayer.
held            any Node the Boot node still holds that never entered the
tree is an orphan by definition, whatever the list above
happens to name. This one needs no contract to be updated
when a new subsystem lands.
layer_order is the answer to 'what covers what' from ARCHITECTURE.md §3,
expressed as an ordering rather than as five magic numbers so that renumbering
the stack cannot silently invert it. A world badge painted across the clock
panel is this assertion failing.
$expect_systems_why: game/core/sim.gd skips a system script that fails to load and only writes a DEBUG line about it, so a build can come up with three systems in it and look calm. These eleven are the parts ARCHITECTURE.md §1 names; a missing one is a script that does not compile.

parts_in_the_tree.$why: required[] below names six subsystems, and it names them because somebody had already been burned by each one. It says nothing about the seventh. [P21] tutorial and [P24] meta are both still unwritten — the day one of them lands, boots, logs 'tutorial ready' and never parents itself, a list-based contract passes it and the gate learns about it from a critic. So this asks the question the other way round: the part folders are READ OFF THE DISK (ARCHITECTURE.md §1: registration is by directory scan, never by editing a shared list) and a part whose scripts appear nowhere in the booted tree is unreachable, listed or not. Fail-closed: a new folder under game/ui/ or game/view/ is covered the day it lands. exempt: needs a real argument, not a name — an entry under 25 characters is refused the same way tools/error_allowlist.txt refuses one.

$orphan_why: Performance.OBJECT_ORPHAN_NODE_COUNT is the engine's own count of nodes that exist and are in no tree. A steady-state boot has none; any number above zero is something that was built and then dropped.

required.why: Nothing is visible without it, and boot's own error path admits as much.
Without a camera in the tree the player is looking at a fixed patch of snow.
The ghost, placement validation and the drag-to-line commit. This is the only path from a mouse to a building.
Clock, heat, vitals, stocks and alerts. A HUD with no children is a panel that failed to build itself.
THE finding. Palette, recipes, tech, blueprints and laws all hang off this node; when it is not in the tree there is no command path from a human into the logistics, research or law systems at all.
The readability lenses are the automation-legibility layer; unreachable, the automation pillar cannot be read even where it works.

layer_order.why: ARCHITECTURE.md §3: the world treatment sits under the interface, a diagnosis beats a decoration, and an open panel is never stabbed through by a world badge. Ordering, not exact numbers, so renumbering cannot invert the stack quietly.

claim_keywords.$why: A log line that announces an install is a claim, and a claim the tree cannot back is exactly the failure mode this part exists to catch. Keywords are matched against any log line containing install/ready/attached/enabled.

forbid_log.why: boot warns and carries on when a subsystem declines. Carrying on is how a build ships with the menu missing.
Same class: a warning nobody reads is not a gate.
